newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-LME FLOOR SHRINKS AGAIN AS DEUTSCHE PULL OUT.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LME FLOOR SHRINKS AGAIN AS DEUTSCHE PULL OUT.

text.p: Almost exactly a year after the metals world was stunned by news of Sumitomo Corp's massive losses in copper, a leading trading company has opted to withdraw from the London Metal Exchange (LME) market floor.

In a surprise move on Wednesday, Deutsche Sharps Pixley, a unit of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, investment arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank, downgraded its membership of the LME - the hub of the world trade in industrial metals.

Deutsche said it relinquished ring membership to become an associate broker clearing (ABC) member. Some of its trading staff had already left the company, although Deutsche would not confirm how many.
"Some of the people associated with the floor, ranging from traders to junior staff, have left," a Deutsche source said.

By moving off-floor, Deutsche will cut costs. To run a floor operation, with telecommunications and associated staff charges, probably costs between one and two million stg a year - or up to around $3.25 million.
Deutsche's new ABC status allows it all the privileges of a ring-dealer, except participating in the twice-daily open-outcry market sessions.
"It is more appropriate for the bank to have its LME membership as an ABC," a Deutsche spokesman said.
Deutsche's move was discussed at Wednesday's LME Board meeting, with the Exchange approving the change in status from 1230 GMT.
LME Chief Executive David King addressed floor traders before the start of afternoon trading, when Deutsche did not staff their booth.
In approving the change, the LME's Board noted that Deutsche was refocussing its LME operations but remained committed to the base metals business, King said.
LME traders were stunned by the development, which reduces the mumber of ring-trading companies to 15. Last November, Lehman Brothers Commodities also pulled off the floor.
The retreat from the floor follows the June 1996 Sumitomo scandal, when the Japanese firm announced losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
"I think that this goes to show that volumes and liquidity are not that great, and that it is difficulty to make money at times," one said.
"It is not exactly a vote of confidence in the market...the banks will always be the first to pull out. Their commitment is to banking, not to metals," another said.
Others doubted whether Deutsche, which only bought Sharps Pixley just over a year ago, was fully committed to floor trading operation, especially in the post-Sumitomo world.
"I think they (Deutsche) were really just after Sharps Pixley's gold book," one senior trader said. Sharps Pixley is one of the big five London bullion gold fixing participants.
Some said the bank decided to shake up metal operations in November with a view to boosting business over the next year, but still struggled.
"They are a bank, and banks should not really be on the floor. After all, they can do big business with producers and consumers and then trade with brokers and pay commission," one said.
Other companies may now take a hard look at their LME floor trading operations.

"It begs the question what benefits to a bank does being a ring-dealer confer...Why maintain a costly operation when you can do the same amount of business (through a broker)," Robin Bhar of LME trader Brandeis said.
However, one of the LME's founding firms - Rudolf Wolff and Co - backed ring-trading.

"We were disappointed at the news, but Rudolf Wolff feels that ring-trading is an integral part of its metals business," William Adams of Wolff said. "Wolff is committed to that, and will continue to provide that service to its customers," he said.
